danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 3
paragraphs: Næste morgen tog fyrst Andrej af sted uden at tage afsked med nogen undtagen greven og uden at vente på, at damerne viste sig.

Det var allerede begyndelsen af juni, da han på hjemvejen kørte ind i birkeskoven, hvor den krogede, gamle eg havde gjort så mærkeligt og uudsletteligt et indtryk på ham. I skoven lød seletøjets bjælder endnu mere dæmpet end seks uger tidligere, for nu var alt tæt, skyggefuldt og tætgroet, og de unge fyretræer, der var spredt i skoven, faldt ikke længere ude af trit med den almene skønhed, men føjede sig efter stemningen og var fine og grønne med bløde, nye skud.

Hele dagen havde været varm. Et sted i det fjerne samlede et uvejr sig, men kun en lille sky havde drysset et par regndråber let hen over vejen og de saftige blade. Venstre side af skoven lå mørk i skygge, den højre glitrede i sollyset, våd og skinnende og næppe bevæget af brisen. Alt stod i blomst, nattergalene sang, og deres stemmer gav genlyd snart nær, snart fjernt.

»Ja, her i denne skov var den eg, som jeg var enig med,« tænkte fyrst Andrej. »Men hvor er den?« undrede han sig igen, mens han kiggede mod venstre side af vejen, og uden at genkende den beundrede han den selvsamme eg, han søgte. Den gamle eg, helt forvandlet, bredte en baldakin af saftig, mørkegrønt løv ud og stod henrevet og let skælvende i den sene eftermiddagssols stråler. Hverken krogede fingre eller gamle ar, hverken gamle tvivl eller sorger var at se nu. Gennem den hårde, hundredårige bark var blade spiret frem, selv hvor der ingen kviste var, blade så frodige, at man næppe kunne tro, den gamle veteran kunne have frembragt dem.

»Ja, det er den samme eg,« tænkte fyrst Andrej, og pludselig greb en uforklarlig forårsfølelse af glæde og fornyelse ham. Alle de bedste øjeblikke i hans liv steg pludselig op i hans hukommelse. Austerlitz med den høje himmel, hans kones døde, bebrejdende ansigt, Pierre ved færgestedet, den pige, der var grebet af nattens skønhed, og den nat selv og månen, og... alt dette stormede pludselig ind i hans bevidsthed.

»Nej, livet er ikke forbi som enogtrediveårig!« besluttede fyrst Andrej pludselig, endeligt og afgørende. »Det er ikke nok for mig at vide, hvad jeg har i mig — alle andre må også vide det: Pierre og den unge pige, der ville flyve af sted op i himlen, alle må kende mig, så mit liv ikke blot leves for mig selv, mens andre lever så fjernt fra det, men så det må afspejle sig i dem alle, og de og jeg kan leve i harmoni!«

Da fyrst Andrej nåede hjem, besluttede han at tage til Sankt Petersborg til efteråret og fandt alle slags grunde til denne beslutning. En hel række fornuftige og logiske overvejelser, der alle viste, at det var nødvendigt for ham at tage til Petersborg, ja endda at genindtræde i tjenesten, dukkede stadig op i hans sind. Han kunne nu ikke forstå, hvordan han overhovedet havde kunnet tvivle på nødvendigheden af at tage aktiv del i livet, lige så lidt som han en måned tidligere havde kunnet forstå, hvordan tanken om at forlade det stille landliv nogensinde kunne falde ham ind. Det forekom ham nu klart, at al hans livserfaring nødvendigvis måtte gå til spilde, medmindre han brugte den på et eller andet arbejde og igen spillede en aktiv rolle i tilværelsen. Han huskede ikke engang, hvordan han tidligere, på grundlag af lignende ynkelige logiske argumenter, havde fundet det indlysende, at han ville nedværdige sig selv, hvis han nu, efter de lektioner livet havde givet ham, tillod sig selv at tro på muligheden af at være nyttig og på muligheden af lykke eller kærlighed. Nu antydede fornuften det stik modsatte. Efter den rejse til Rjazan fandt han landlivet kedeligt; hans tidligere sysler interesserede ham ikke mere, og ofte, når han sad alene i sit arbejdsværelse, rejste han sig, gik hen til spejlet og betragtede længe sit eget ansigt. Så vendte han sig mod portrættet af sin afdøde Lise, der med håret krøllet à la grecque så ømt og muntert på ham ud af den forgyldte ramme. Hun sagde nu ikke længere de forfærdelige ord til ham, men så blot enkelt, muntert og nysgerrigt på ham. Og fyrst Andrej krydsede armene bag ryggen og vandrede længe op og ned i stuen, snart rynkende brynene, snart smilende, mens han tænkte over de irrationelle, uudsigelige tanker — hemmelige som en forbrydelse — der forandrede hele hans liv og var forbundet med Pierre, med berømmelse, med pigen ved vinduet, egen og kvindelig skønhed og kærlighed. Og hvis nogen kom ind i hans rum i sådanne øjeblikke, var han særlig kold, streng og frem for alt ubehageligt logisk.
»Min kære,« sagde fyrstinde Marja, der kom ind på sådanne tidspunkter, »lille Nikolaj kan ikke komme ud i dag, det er meget koldt.«

»Hvis det var varmt,« svarede fyrst Andrej på sådanne tidspunkter meget tørt til sin søster, »kunne han gå ud i sin kittel, men da det er koldt, må han have varmt tøj på, som er lavet til det formål. Det følger af, at det er koldt; og ikke at et barn, der har brug for frisk luft, skal blive hjemme,« tilføjede han med ekstrem logik, som om han straffede nogen for de hemmelige, ulogiske følelser, der rørte sig i ham.
I sådanne øjeblikke tænkte fyrstinde Marja, at åndeligt arbejde udtørrer mænd.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Next morning, having said goodbye to no one but the count and without waiting for the ladies to appear, Prince Andrew set off for home.

It was already the beginning of June when, on his return journey, he drove into the birch forest where the gnarled old oak had made such a strange and memorable impression on him. In the forest the harness bells sounded even more muffled than they had six weeks before, for now everything was thick, shady, and dense. The young firs scattered through the forest no longer clashed with the general beauty but, blending in with the mood around them, were delicately green with fluffy new shoots.

The whole day had been hot. Somewhere a storm was gathering, but only a small cloud had sprinkled a few raindrops on the road and the juicy leaves. The left side of the forest was dark in shadow; the right side sparkled in the sunlight, wet and glistening and barely stirred by the breeze. Everything was in bloom, the nightingales trilled, and their songs echoed now near, now far away.

"Yes — it was here in this forest, with that oak I agreed with," thought Prince Andrew. "But where is it?" he wondered again, looking to the left side of the road, and without recognizing it, he gazed in admiration at the very oak he had been looking for. The old oak, completely transformed, spread a canopy of rich, dark-green foliage and stood swaying gently, almost trembling, in the rays of the evening sun. Neither gnarled fingers nor old scars nor old doubts and sorrows were anywhere in evidence. Through the tough, century-old bark — even where there were no branches — leaves had sprouted, so fresh and vigorous it was hard to believe the old veteran could have produced them.

"Yes, it is the same oak," thought Prince Andrew, and all at once he was seized by an unreasoning springtime feeling of joy and renewal. All the best moments of his life suddenly rose to his memory. Austerlitz with the vast heavens, his wife's dead, reproachful face, Pierre at the ferry, that girl thrilled by the beauty of the night, and that night itself, and the moon — all of it rushed suddenly into his mind.

"No, life is not over at thirty-one!" Prince Andrew suddenly decided, finally and irrevocably. "It's not enough for me to know what I have inside me — everyone must know it: Pierre, and that young girl who wanted to fly into the sky — everyone must know me, so that my life is not lived for myself alone, apart from everyone else, but so that it is reflected in them all, and they and I may live in harmony!"

On reaching home, Prince Andrew decided to go to Petersburg that autumn and found all sorts of reasons to justify this decision. A whole series of sensible, logical arguments showing that it was essential to go — and even to re-enter the service — kept springing up in his mind. He could not now understand how he had ever doubted the necessity of taking an active part in life, just as a month ago he hadn't understood how the idea of leaving the country could enter his head. It now seemed clear that all his experience of life would be senselessly wasted unless he put it to some use and played an active role again. He didn't even remember how, on the strength of similar flimsy logic, it had previously seemed obvious that he'd be debasing himself if he allowed himself — after the lessons life had taught him — to believe again in the possibility of being useful, and in the possibility of happiness or love. Now reason pointed in exactly the opposite direction. After that trip to Ryazan he found country life dull; his old pursuits no longer interested him, and often, sitting alone in his study, he would get up, go to the mirror, and stare at his own face for a long time. Then he would turn away to look at the portrait of his dead Lise, who, with her hair curled a la grecque, gazed out of the gilt frame tenderly and cheerfully. She no longer spoke those terrible words to him but simply looked at him — merrily, curiously, and questioningly. And Prince Andrew, clasping his hands behind his back, would pace the room for ages, now frowning, now smiling, as he pondered those irrational, inexpressible thoughts — secret as a crime — that altered his entire life and were connected with Pierre, with fame, with the girl at the window, the oak, and woman's beauty and love. And if anyone came into his room at such moments, he was particularly cold, stern, and above all unpleasantly logical.
"My dear," Princess Mary would say, entering at such a moment, "little Nicholas can't go out today — it's very cold."

"If it were hot," Prince Andrew would reply at such times very drily to his sister, "he could go out in his smock. But since it's cold, he must wear warm clothes, which were designed for that purpose. That is the logical consequence of it being cold — not that a child who needs fresh air should be kept indoors." He would add this with exaggerated logic, as if punishing someone for those secret, illogical emotions stirring within him.
At such moments Princess Mary would think how intellectual work dries men up.
